messages.content:
You are checking one scene of a novel for one specific continuity error.

The book had already established this, earlier or elsewhere:
- (building) "She knew these things because she had been inside this building every night for four nights."

A past rewrite of this scene contradicted it. The error looked like this:
- (claire) "the sound Maren had heard through eleven nights of dreaming"
(Summary: Maren dreamed Claire's captivity for four nights, but claire says she heard Claire "through eleven nights of dreaming".)

Here is a NEW draft of the same scene:
<scene>
The shape resolved into a woman.

Head down, chin on her chest, a white pillowcase over her face gone gray with the mark of her mouth where she'd breathed through it for nine days. Zip-tied at the wrists to the arms of a metal folding chair. Bare feet on concrete. The space heater's coils glowed orange at the far wall, throwing enough heat to keep her alive and not enough to make her warm, and Maren understood that calibration the way she understood the smell. She'd been in this room before. She'd worn that pillowcase. She knew the exact weight of the fabric when it sucked tight against an open mouth.

"Claire." She said it at the volume you'd use across a pillow. "Claire Renaud. My name is Maren. I'm with the Multnomah County DA's office and your sister Marie sent me."

The head came up.

Not fast. The body underneath had learned not to move fast. But it came up, and the pillowcase turned toward the phone light, and a sound came out of her that wasn't a word, wasn't anything, just the involuntary noise a throat makes when the thing it has stopped hoping for walks through the door it has stopped watching.

Maren crossed the fifteen feet.

She went to her knees on the concrete and set the phone face-up on the floor so the light bounced off the metal ceiling and filled the room gray instead of stabbing. Then she took the hem of the pillowcase in both hands. "I'm going to take this off now. I'm here. I've got you."

The fabric lifted away.

Auburn hair matted to a skull. A face Maren had memorized from a hospital ID badge and a sister's phone and could not have prepared for, because the badge photo had a gap-toothed smile and this had cracked lips and a crust of salt under both eyes where the tears had dried and dried again. Claire's pupils blew wide in the dim and found Maren's face and locked there.

"You're real," Claire said. Her voice came out in pieces.

"I'm real."

"I kept—" The breath hitched. "I kept making you up. I made up so many people."

"Not this time." Maren's hands were already at the zip ties, testing the lock, finding the tongue. She looked back over her shoulder. "Hank."

He was at the threshold with his hands open at his sides. He hadn't come in. For a second he didn't move at all, and she watched something cross his face in the gray light, something she had no name for yet and would understand later, the particular stillness of a man standing in a doorway he has already stood in from the wrong side.

"Multi-tool," she said.

It broke him loose. He crossed the room and crouched and had the tool open and the blade sawing through the first tie before she'd finished asking, and his hands were steady, and Claire flinched at the nearness of him until Maren put her own palm flat against the woman's sternum.

"He's with me. He's the one who got the door."

The first tie parted. Claire's right arm dropped off the chair arm like a thing that had forgotten it was attached to her. Hank moved to the second without a word, and Maren kept her hand on Claire's chest and felt the heart going under it, fast and thin and alive, hammering against her palm.

Rook came then. Pushed her gray muzzle under Claire's slack hand where it hung, and pressed, and held it there, and made the high thin sound in her throat that she made for her own people. Claire's fingers moved. Found the dog's ear. Closed on it.

"That's Rook," Maren said. "She knew you were in here before we did."

The second tie gave. Both of Claire's arms were free now and she brought them in against her body, slow, like someone testing whether the parts still worked, and then she was shaking, the whole frame of her coming apart in increments, and Maren got an arm around her shoulders and took the weight.

"Okay," she said into the matted hair. "Okay. You can do that now. I've got you. You can do that now."

She was aware of Hank rising, of him stepping back to the doorway, putting his body between the two women and the dark toward the house a quarter mile east. Taking the watch. She didn't look at him. She had her hand spread on Claire Renaud's back, feeling the sobs come up through the ribs, and she was counting them the way she'd once counted a hooded woman's breaths in a dream she couldn't wake from, except this was flesh under her hand and this was happening and this woman was going to see Marie before morning.

Eleven years. Eleven years of sitting in beige rooms with women after. After the rape kit. After the autopsy. After the protective order that came too late or not at all. She had built an entire self out of arriving after, had told herself the math justified it, had driven away from a girl on 82nd Avenue because she had nothing left and the next week's cases needed her whole.

This was during.

She hadn't known the difference would land in her body like this. Like something cracking open that she'd mortared shut years ago to keep standing. Her own eyes were streaming and she let them.

"Marie said she'd know if you were gone," she said. "She said she'd feel it. She was right."

Claire's hand tightened in Rook's fur. "She always thinks she's right."

A sound came out of Maren that was half laugh, surprised out of her, wet. "Yeah. Well."

"Is she—" Claire pulled back far enough to find Maren's face again, and the terror underneath was still there, the animal part that didn't trust the light yet. "Is he here? Is he coming back?"

From the doorway, without turning, Hank spoke for the first time since the truck.

"He's not coming back in this building."
</scene>

Does the new draft make the same error — does it assert something that contradicts what was established, in the way described? A draft that simply leaves the fact out does not make the error.

Answer with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"verdict": "reintroduced" | "consistent" | "not_present", "evidence": "<verbatim sentence from the new draft that decides it, or empty for not_present>"}

"reintroduced": the new draft contradicts the established fact.
"consistent": the new draft states the fact and agrees with what was established.
"not_present": the new draft does not touch the fact either way.
